title: Fold and Mirror
context: Grade 4, and the chapter's opening question comes back here. An adult sees paper being folded. What is actually being settled is that a line of symmetry is tested by folding and not guessed by looking, which is why a rectangle's diagonal, which looks as though it should work, is a trap: fold along it and the corners stick out. Every mirror line in the section's printed examples stands upright, though one exercise later lays a mirror across, and the box asking which letters look the same in a mirror never says which mirror it means, so this tool names the upright one and shows the other beside it.

writeup.why: Fold a figure to find out whether its halves match, and stand it by a mirror to see where its image goes.
writeup.look: A paper figure on a table with a fold line across it, a tally beside it, and a mirror bay on squared paper at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Fold and Mirror' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the folds kept against the folds tried, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one only when a fold matches and is kept and the second with every fold made. In the mirror bay it carries the corners placed against the corners of the shape, and on the fourth phase the letters sorted against the letters tried. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The table fills the left of the working area, 600 by 470 at 64,214, on the panel colour, and holds up to three paper figures side by side, each drawn as a flat deep blue shape with its own tally card under it. The fold line is drawn solid in sky blue while it is being tried, and it can be dragged and turned to any position across a figure. The fold control turns one side of the paper over onto the other along it, the turned half drawn sky blue: where the halves match exactly, the fold sets hard, the line is redrawn dotted in reddish purple and kept, and the tally takes one; where any part sticks out past the other half, the overhang glows sky blue, the line stays solid and the paper opens back out by itself. The mirror bay stands at the right, 470 by 470 at 680,214, on near-black squared paper, with an upright mirror line drawn dotted in reddish purple down its middle. A shape placed on one side sends a thin amber string from each of its corners straight across to the mirror line, counting squares, and on by the same number of squares beyond it, and the image is drawn in sky blue at the ends of the strings, turned the other way round. The lying mirror waits at the foot of the bay and can be laid across it, and when it is, the strings run straight up or down to it instead. The letter tray runs along the foot of the working area, 1086 by 40 at 64,690, holding the twenty-six capitals in one plain face without tails or serifs; a letter dragged beside a mirror has its image drawn behind the mirror line, and with both mirrors open its two images stand side by side. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is a word pad wherever a fold or a pair is judged, with keys reading yes, no, line of symmetry and not a line of symmetry, and two keys naming the mirror, upright or lying across. It is twelve number keys three across wherever lines are counted or squares from the mirror line are asked for, and the letter tray itself wherever letters are sorted. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion. A length being measured, walked, added or named, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted. The second thing set beside the first, a fold being tried, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter and the larger angle between clock hands, is sky blue. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a point is a round dot, a line carries an arrowhead at each end, a ray a dot and one arrowhead and a segment a dot at each end, a measured length carries its number, a hidden edge is dashed and a line of symmetry is dotted, before any of them is told by a colour. A dotted line always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is drawn solid until it is kept, so nothing else on any stage of this chapter is ever dotted. A dotted line on this stage always means a true line of symmetry or a mirror line, and a fold being tried is always solid, so a line is never shown as known to work before it has been folded. The mirror stands upright unless the question lays it across, as one printed exercise does, and then the lying mirror is drawn across the bay and named.
writeup.finish: The card shows the figures the child folded with every kept fold drawn dotted, and the letters sorted into the two rows beside the upright mirror.

phases.win: the halves lie exactly together, the fold sets hard, and the line is kept as a line of symmetry
phases.does: sets the fold line, folds, and looks for any part that sticks out
phases.goal: a fold is a line of symmetry only when one half fits exactly over the other
phases.says: Fold it along your line. Does every part fit, or does something stick out?
phases.check: Look again at the temple on the chapter's opening page. Seen from the front, where would you fold a drawing of it so the halves match?
phases.feels: a fold keeps only if nothing at all sticks out
phases.hands: Fold a sheet of paper in half, cut a shape along the open edge and unfold it. Ask where the fold is and why the halves match. Then cut a shape from an unfolded sheet, fold it through what looks like its middle, and look for any part that sticks out.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: does any part stick out after the fold? Second rung, the phase's: where would the fold have to be for the halves to meet? Third rung: the figure is cut to a plain square and folded across its middle before the harder figure comes back. The word pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: a line that crosses the whole figure looks as though it divides it fairly, and the eye does not measure the two parts.
wrong.move: calls a line across a rectangle near its top a line of symmetry, because it runs right across the figure.
wrong.screen: the fold is made along the child's line, the thin top strip turning down onto the rest, and the long part below sticks out past it and glows sky blue. The line stays solid, the paper opens back out, and the true fold across the middle is then tried and kept, drawn dotted. The child's answer stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the N has an upright stroke on each side, and two matching strokes look like two matching halves.
wrong.move: folds a capital N down its middle and calls the fold a line of symmetry, because each half has one upright stroke.
wrong.screen: the fold is made down the middle of the N, and the slanting stroke of the turned half lands crossing the other half's slant instead of lying on it, both glowing sky blue where they miss. The line stays solid, the paper opens back out, and the child's answer stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a paper figure on the table with the fold line lying across it
phases.soWhat: A fold is a line of symmetry only when one half fits exactly over the other.

phases.win: the square's tally stops at four, the rectangle's at two with its diagonal turned away, and the letter's at none
phases.does: tries folds down, across and corner to corner on each figure and reads the tallies
phases.goal: a figure can have one line of symmetry, several, or none, and each is found by folding
phases.says: Try every fold you can. How many lines does each one keep?
phases.check: How many lines of symmetry does a capital H have? Fold a paper one to check.
phases.feels: a figure keeps every fold that matches and no others, and some keep none at all
phases.hands: Give each group a paper square, a long paper rectangle and a cut-out capital F. Ask them to find every fold that makes matching halves, and to mark each one with a dotted pencil line. Ask why the rectangle's corner to corner fold does not work when the square's does.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which folds have you tried? Second rung, the phase's: have you tried the folds from corner to corner? Third rung: the figure is cut to the square, and the fold line is turned a step at a time while the tally keeps count. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the diagonal cuts the rectangle into two triangles of exactly the same size, and a square's diagonals both work.
wrong.move: counts a long rectangle's diagonal as a line of symmetry and says it has four, like a square.
wrong.screen: the fold is made along the diagonal and the turned triangle lands with two corners sticking out past the other half, both glowing sky blue, and the line stays solid. The square beside it folds along its diagonal and matches, so the two diagonal folds are seen side by side. The rectangle's tally stays at two and the child's four stays in the slot.

wrong.why: folds down and across are the ones a hand makes first, and a slanting fold does not feel like a fold of the same kind.
wrong.move: stops after the upright and across folds and misses the slanting ones.
wrong.screen: the fold line is turned a step at a time round the square, and at each slanting position where the halves meet, the fold sets and is kept, the tally climbing past two to four. The child's count stays in the slot beside the tally, nothing marked.

phases.screen: a square, a long rectangle and a capital letter F side by side, each with an empty tally
phases.soWhat: A figure can have one line of symmetry, several or none; a rectangle that is not a square has two, and a square has four.
phases.concept: More than one line, or none

phases.win: every corner of the image lands at the end of its string and the image stands turned the other way round
phases.does: runs a string from each corner to the mirror line, carries it on the same distance, and places the image
phases.goal: an image sits the same distance behind the mirror line as the object, turned the other way round
phases.says: How far is this corner from the mirror? Go the same distance behind it.
phases.check: On squared paper, draw an upright mirror line and a dot five squares to its left. Where does the image of the dot go?
phases.feels: every corner goes as far behind the line as it stood in front, so the near side stays near and the far side stays far
phases.hands: Stand a mirror upright on a line drawn across squared paper. Put a counter three squares in front of it and ask how far behind the mirror its image seems to be. Then draw a shape with one corner close to the line and one far from it, and place its image corner by corner, counting squares from the line each time.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many squares is this corner from the mirror line? Second rung, the phase's: how many squares behind the line must its image be? Third rung: the shape is cut to a single dot, and its string is run across before the whole shape comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: an image in a mirror seems to sit on the glass, and the distance behind it cannot be touched.
wrong.move: draws the image right up against the mirror line, or at a different distance from it than the shape.
wrong.screen: a string runs from each corner of the shape straight across to the mirror line and on by the same number of squares beyond it, the squares counted aloud on each side. The image is drawn at the ends of the strings in sky blue, and the child's image stays where it was placed, its corners short of the string ends.

wrong.why: sliding a shape across is the simplest way to put it on the other side, and it keeps the shape looking the right way round.
wrong.move: slides the shape across the line without turning it round, so the image faces the same way as the shape.
wrong.screen: the strings run from each corner, and the corner nearest the mirror lands nearest it on the other side while the farthest lands farthest, so the image comes out turned the other way round. The child's slid copy stays beside it, and the corner that stood nearest the mirror is lit in it, now sitting farthest from the line.

phases.screen: a shape on squared paper beside an upright mirror line, with the distance strings coiled
phases.soWhat: A mirror image sits the same distance behind the mirror line as the shape is in front of it, turned the other way round.

phases.win: the sorted letters settle in two rows, and the lying mirror moves some of them from one row to the other
phases.does: places letters beside the upright mirror one at a time and sorts them into same and turned, then tries the lying mirror
phases.goal: a letter looks the same in an upright mirror only if it has an upright line of symmetry
phases.says: Does it look the same in the mirror? Now try the other mirror.
phases.check: Which of the capital letters H, K, O and W look the same in an upright mirror? Which look the same in a mirror lying across?
phases.feels: which letters match depends on which way the mirror stands
phases.hands: Write the capital letters large on cards. Hold each beside an upright mirror and sort them into two piles, looks the same and faces the other way. Then lay the mirror flat under each card and sort again. Ask which letters changed piles, and why the question has to say which mirror.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which mirror is the question about? Second rung, the phase's: does the letter have a line of symmetry running the same way as that mirror? Third rung: the tray is cut to two letters, A and B, and each is tried in both mirrors before the rest come back. The letter tray and the word pad stay open.

wrong.why: the box asking for these letters never says which mirror it means, so any letter that looked the same in any mirror seems to belong.
wrong.move: names the letters that look the same without saying which mirror, mixing B and C, which match in a mirror lying across, with A and M, which match in an upright one.
wrong.screen: each of the child's letters is set beside the upright mirror and then above the lying mirror, and its two images are drawn side by side. The letters settle into two rows headed upright and lying across, A and M in one and B and C in the other, and the child's list stays in the slot with the mirror keys lit beside it.

wrong.why: turning a card round is how a letter is usually flipped in the hand, and N comes through that unchanged.
wrong.move: says N looks the same in an upright mirror, because it looks the same turned half way round.
wrong.screen: N is set beside the upright mirror and its image is drawn behind the line point for point, facing the other way. The child's N turned half way round is drawn beside it, the two stand plainly different, and nothing is marked.

phases.screen: the letter tray beside the upright mirror, with the lying mirror set aside
phases.soWhat: In an upright mirror, a letter looks the same only if it has an upright line of symmetry: in plain capitals, A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y. In a mirror lying across, B, C, D, E, H, I, K, O and X do.
phases.concept: Letters that look the same in a mirror

writeup.delight: The second phase, the moment the fold line is turned onto the square's diagonal. The paper turns over along it, one triangle lying down exactly onto the other with not a hair showing, the fold sets and the line turns from solid to dotted. Drag the same line onto the long rectangle's diagonal and fold, and two corners swing out past the other half and glow, the line stays solid, and the paper opens back out by itself. The two diagonals can be tried one after the other as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a paper figure lies on the table with a solid fold line lying across it and its tally card empty. On the second a square, a long rectangle and a capital F lie side by side on the table, each with its own empty tally card, and the fold line rests on the square. On the third a shape stands on the squared paper of the mirror bay, to the left of the upright mirror line, drawn dotted, with a string coiled at each of its corners. On the fourth the letter tray stands open along the foot, the upright mirror stands in the bay and the lying mirror waits at the bay's foot. The running count at the top left holds the folds kept against the folds tried, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the fold line, or the square's tally card, or the corner nearest the mirror, or the first letter in the tray, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks whether the halves will fit. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any figure, any fold, and any shape or letter in the mirror bay, with the upright mirror and the lying mirror both open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on folds that match, figures with several lines of symmetry or none, images the same distance behind a mirror line, and letters in an upright mirror.
voiceLines: A paper shape and a fold line across it. Will the two halves fit?
Fold it along your line. Does every part fit, or does something stick out?
Try every fold you can. How many lines does each one keep?
How far is this corner from the mirror? Go the same distance behind it.
Does it look the same in the mirror? Now try the other mirror.
A new shape. Guess its folds, then test every one.
Free play. Any shape, any fold, any letter, with both mirrors open.
Open it out and fold again slowly, watching for anything that sticks out.
Every fold tested, every image placed at its distance, and the mirror named for every letter.

observations.why: One half has to fit exactly over the other for the fold to be a line of symmetry.
observations.soWhat: A line of symmetry is found by folding, and a line that only looks central may not be one.
observations.observe: A fold set hard only when nothing stuck out past the other half.

observations.why: Each fold that lays one half exactly on the other is kept, and different figures have different numbers of those.
observations.soWhat: A figure can have several lines of symmetry, one, or none, and a rectangle that is not a square does not fold along its diagonal.
observations.observe: The square kept four folds, the long rectangle two, and the capital F none.

observations.why: The image of each point sits as far behind the line as the point is in front, straight across.
observations.soWhat: A mirror image is the same distance behind the mirror line as the object, turned the other way round.
observations.observe: Every string ran the same number of squares behind the mirror line as in front of it.

observations.why: An upright mirror swaps left and right, and a mirror lying across swaps top and bottom.
observations.soWhat: Which letters look the same depends on which way the mirror stands, so a question about them must say which mirror.
observations.observe: Some letters moved from one row to the other when the lying mirror took the upright mirror's place.

source_tool.description: A paper figure lies on the table in the middle of the stage. A fold line can be dragged and turned to any position, and folding lays one side over the other: where the halves match exactly the fold sets hard and is kept as a line of symmetry, and where any part sticks out the overhang glows and the paper opens again. A tally beside the figure keeps every fold that matched, so a figure with several lines of symmetry collects them all and a figure with none collects nothing. A mirror bay stands an upright mirror line on squared paper. A shape placed on one side sends a measuring string from each of its corners straight across to the mirror line, and its image is drawn the same distance behind the line, turned the other way round, with each string carried through to its matching corner. A letter tray sets capital letters beside the upright mirror, and each image either matches its letter or is shown facing the other way. A second mirror, lying across under a letter, can be set beside the upright one, so the answer is seen to depend on which way the mirror stands.
source_tool.art_direction: Folded paper beside an upright mirror / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a drawing board with a ruler and a point stamp, a tracing finger and a flag, a walker and a string, square tiles on squared paper, a pair of compasses with a metal point and a pencil arm, a sheet of paper that folds, an upright mirror, solids on a turntable, flat nets that fold up, hinged arms, a clock face and a grid of pictures.

A line is always drawn with an arrowhead at each end, a ray with a dot at its end point and one arrowhead, and a line segment with a dot at each end. No stroke is ever left with a bare end that could be read as either.

A point is drawn as one small dot of one size wherever it appears, named by a capital letter beside it. Within one figure no letter ever names two different things, and a figure never renames a part it has already named.

Every labelled length is one the figure could really have, and every figure is drawn to scale with its labels. A triangle drawn with a square corner carries lengths such as three, four and five, and a stepped shape's sides close up exactly.
A figure on squared paper sits exactly on the grid lines, with every side along a line and every square either wholly inside it or wholly outside it.

A circle drawn to show its parts has its centre marked as a dot and named. Every radius is drawn from that dot to the curve, and a diameter always passes exactly through the dot. A circle that is a view of a solid carries a dot only where the solid has a point, so a cylinder seen from above is a plain circle.
A right angle carries a small square corner mark, and every other angle an arc drawn close to its vertex between the arms.

A line of symmetry and a mirror line are drawn dotted and lie exactly where the fold falls. A fold line being tried is drawn solid and turns dotted only once the fold is kept. Every mirror line stands upright unless the frame says it lies across, and an image sits exactly as far behind the line as the thing in front of it, turned the other way round.
A solid is drawn with its hidden edges dashed. Views of one solid are drawn at one scale, so the front view and the side view of a box are exactly the same height.

Clock hands point exactly at the numbers and the minute hand is the longer. Where the angle between the hands is shown, both angles are shaded and the smaller one is outlined. No clock is set to six o'clock or twelve o'clock.
A grid carries its row numbers down the left edge and its column numbers across the top, and each picture in it appears once.
A shape, a side or a part is told apart by its label first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a line, a point, a square or a part the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The figure being studied, every line, segment, ray, side, outline, circle, angle arm and visible edge of a solid, is deep blue. Every point, end point, corner dot, vertex dot and the centre dot of a circle is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter that opens on the point cannot afford a frame where a point has to be hunted for. A length being measured, walked, added or named, the tape, the walker's sum, a radius being measured, and every angle arc and square corner mark, is amber. The unit squares that cover an area, the flood inside a closed figure and a face of a solid being counted are green. A line of symmetry or a mirror line is reddish purple and always dotted, so a dotted line always means a true line of symmetry. Sky blue is the second thing set beside the first: a fold being tried, drawn solid until it is kept, a mirror image, the other half of a fold, a chord that is not a diameter, and the larger angle between clock hands. A hidden edge of a solid is grey and dashed, and grey is used for nothing else. Every grid line, ruler tick, bracket, guide line and table rule is near-black chrome. All of that holds in greyscale, because a point is a round dot, a measured length carries its number, a line of symmetry is dotted, a fold being tried is solid and a hidden edge is dashed.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Open it out and fold again slowly, watching for anything that sticks out.
voice.onNext: A new shape. Guess its folds, then test every one.
voice.opening: A paper shape and a fold line across it. Will the two halves fit?
voice.onFinish: Every fold tested, every image placed at its distance, and the mirror named for every letter.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any shape, any fold, any letter, with both mirrors open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After paint has been blotted inside a folded sheet and the sheet opened, and before any dotted line on the page is judged. The tool is what folds a figure along a line the child has chosen and keeps the fold only if the halves match, which a dotted line printed on a page cannot do.

answer_key.rule: A figure is symmetric if folding it along a line makes one part fit exactly over the other, and that line is a line of symmetry. Some figures have one line of symmetry, some have more than one, and some have none. A rectangle has two, down its middle and across its middle, and its diagonal is not one; a square has four. A mirror image appears on the other side of the mirror line, the same distance from it as the object, turned the other way round, and the mirror line is a line of symmetry between them. A letter looks the same in an upright mirror only if it has an upright line of symmetry: A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y in plain capitals. In a mirror lying across under the letter, the letters with a line of symmetry across their middle look the same instead.
answer_key.wrong: The fold is opened and made again slowly, with any part that sticks out glowing, and in the mirror bay the strings are run from each corner to the line and on again. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The fold runs straight down through the middle of the stem and the middle of the top bar.
Each half of the bar is the same length, and each half of the stem is the same width.
So one half fits exactly over the other, and the fold is a line of symmetry of the T.
items.answer: Yes. The left half fits exactly over the right half, so the fold is a line of symmetry
items.question: A paper cut-out of the capital letter T is folded along an upright line down the middle of its stem. Do the halves match?
items.checkpoint: A fold is a line of symmetry only when one half fits exactly over the other.
items.misconception: Judging by eye that a line looks central, without checking that every part fits.

steps: An upright fold and a fold across each lay two arms exactly onto the other two.
A slanting fold through the inside corners where two arms meet lays each arm onto its neighbour.
There are two such slanting folds, so the plus sign has four lines of symmetry.
items.answer: Four: one upright, one across, and two slanting ones through the corners where the arms meet
items.question: A plus sign has four arms of equal length and equal width. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
items.checkpoint: A figure can have more than one line of symmetry, and every one is found by folding.
items.misconception: Stopping at the upright and across folds and missing the two slanting ones.

steps: An image is the same distance from the mirror line as the object.
The dot is four squares from the line, so its image is four squares from it too.
It sits on the other side, to the right, and at the same height, because the string runs straight across.
items.answer: Four squares to the right of the mirror line, level with the dot
items.question: On squared paper, a dot sits four squares to the left of an upright mirror line. Where does its image sit?
items.checkpoint: An image sits the same distance behind the mirror line as the object, on the other side.
items.misconception: Placing the image right up against the mirror line, or the same distance from the edge of the paper.

steps: In an upright mirror, the left and the right of a letter swap over.
A and V each have an upright line of symmetry, so swapping left and right leaves them the same.
B and D have no upright line of symmetry, so their images face the other way.
items.answer: A and V. Each has an upright line of symmetry, while B and D face the other way in the mirror
items.question: Which of the capital letters A, B, D and V look the same in an upright mirror?
items.checkpoint: A letter looks the same in an upright mirror only if it has an upright line of symmetry.
items.misconception: Answering without saying which mirror, when B and D look the same in a mirror lying across.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A building seen from the front has a left half that matches its right half exactly. Where is its line of symmetry?
items.final_answer: One upright line straight down the middle of the front

items.question: A shape is folded along a line, and one corner sticks out past the other half. Is the fold a line of symmetry?
items.final_answer: No, because the halves do not fit exactly over each other

items.question: How many lines of symmetry does the capital letter F have?
items.final_answer: None. No fold makes one half fit exactly over the other

items.question: A long rectangle is folded corner to corner along its diagonal. Do the halves match, and how many lines of symmetry does it have?
items.final_answer: No, the corners stick out. It has two lines of symmetry, one down its middle and one across its middle

items.question: A triangle stands to the left of an upright mirror line. Its nearest corner is three squares from the line and its farthest is five. How far from the line are those corners in the image?
items.final_answer: Three squares and five squares, on the right of the line, so the image faces the other way

items.question: Two copies of the capital letter R stand on either side of an upright mirror line, both facing the same way. Is one the reflection of the other?
items.final_answer: No. In an upright mirror the image of R faces the other way, so a reflection would be turned round

items.question: Which of the capital letters C, H, K, O and U look the same in an upright mirror?
items.final_answer: H, O and U, which each have an upright line of symmetry

items.question: The capital letter E is held beside an upright mirror, and then above a mirror lying flat under it. In which mirror does it look the same?
items.final_answer: In the mirror lying flat under it, because E has a line of symmetry across its middle. In the upright mirror it faces the other way

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: drags and turns to any position on the figure
lays one side over the other and keeps the fold only if the halves match
lights any part that sticks out past the other half
stands a mirror line straight up on squared paper
run from each corner straight across to the mirror line and on to the image
sets capital letters beside the mirror
sets a second mirror across under a letter, beside the upright one

teaching_notes: Blot paint in a folded sheet before the tool is opened, and let the class see that the fold is exactly where the two halves meet. Then judge every dotted line by folding, never by eye. The printed exercise holds a rectangle with a dotted line along its diagonal, and it looks right and is not; fold one and the corners stick out. The opening story asks whether you can draw the temple's line of symmetry and does not say which view. From the front it is one upright line down the middle; the plan from above has nine sides and nine lines, and a child who says so is right too. Every mirror line in the section's examples stands upright, and the box asking for letters that look the same in a mirror never says which mirror. Name it: in an upright mirror, the letters are A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y in plain capitals. Then lay a mirror flat under a letter and let the class find that B, C, D, E and K now look the same instead, so the question needs its mirror named.
generation_prompt: Build a folding and mirror tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A paper figure lies in the middle of the working area, drawn as a flat filled shape. A fold line, drawn solid while it is being tried, can be dragged and turned to any position across it. A fold control animates one side of the paper turning over onto the other: where the halves match exactly, the fold sets, the line is redrawn dotted and it is kept in a tally beside the figure; where any part sticks out, the overhang glows, the line stays solid and the paper opens back out, with nothing marked. The tally collects every matching fold, so a square collects four, a long rectangle two and a capital F none. A mirror bay at the right stands an upright mirror line, drawn dotted, on squared paper. A shape placed on one side sends a thin string from each corner straight across to the line and on the same distance beyond it, and its image is drawn at the ends of the strings, turned the other way round. A letter tray sets plain capital letters beside the mirror and draws each letter's image, and a lying mirror can be set across under a letter beside the upright one, so both images show together. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Choose a fold line and fold. If every part fits, it is a line of symmetry. Try every fold you can. Measure from each corner to the mirror line. Put the image the same distance behind it.
